questions.stem: An auditor reviews the switch configuration below. Which finding is MOST important?
questions.exhibit:
username netadmin privilege 15 secret 9 $9$h3YpQ0vXbN2kLs$Wq...
username backup privilege 1 password 0 Backup2026
!
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh

options.text: The backup account's password is stored in plain text
options.rationale: Correct: 'password 0' keeps it readable in the config; 'secret' would hash it.

options.text: Accounts live on this one device, so managing them doesn't scale
options.rationale: A real limitation of local accounts, but not the security finding here.

options.text: SSH logins on the VTY lines are checked locally
options.rationale: True, and acceptable; that is what 'login local' does.

options.text: The netadmin secret can be read back as plain text
options.rationale: Type 9 secrets are hashed.

questions.explanation: Local authentication stores accounts on the device itself, created with 'username NAME privilege 15 secret PASS' and applied to lines with 'login local'. 'secret' is stored hashed; 'password' is not, and type 0 is plain text. Local accounts also don't scale, because each device holds its own.
questions.discriminator_tested: 'secret' is hashed; 'password' is not; local accounts don't scale.

questions.stem: A user types a username, enters a password and a token code, is allowed into the finance share but not the HR share, and each file opened is logged. Which sequence names these four steps?

options.text: Identification, authentication, authorization, accounting
options.rationale: Correct: claim, prove, permit, record.

options.text: Authentication, identification, authorization, accounting
options.rationale: The identity is claimed before it can be proven.

options.text: Identification, authorization, authentication, accounting
options.rationale: Permissions are decided only after identity is proven.

options.text: Identification, authentication, accounting, authorization
options.rationale: Logging what was done comes after access is decided.

questions.explanation: The iAAA model is identification (who are you?), authentication (prove it), authorization (what may you do?), and accounting (what did you do?).
questions.discriminator_tested: iAAA: who are you, prove it, what may you do, what did you do.

questions.stem: At a secure door, a user's badge, PIN, and fingerprint are checked, and the door then opens to the lobby but not to the lab. Which part of that process was authentication?

options.text: Checking the badge, PIN, and fingerprint
options.rationale: Correct: verifying the claimed identity with factors.

options.text: Deciding the lobby is allowed but the lab is not
options.rationale: That is authorization.

options.text: Logging the time the user entered the lobby
options.rationale: That is accounting.

options.text: Printing the user's name on the badge
options.rationale: Issuing a badge isn't verifying anyone.

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies a claimed identity using one or more factors (something you know, have, or are). It proves identity but says nothing yet about permissions; that is authorization.
questions.discriminator_tested: Authentication proves identity; it says nothing about permissions.

questions.stem: Which two sign-in methods count as MFA? (Choose two.)

options.text: A password plus a code from an authenticator app
options.rationale: Correct: something you know plus something you have.

options.text: A smart card plus a PIN
options.rationale: Correct: something you have plus something you know.

options.text: A password plus a security question
options.rationale: Both are things you know: one category.

options.text: Two different passwords
options.rationale: Still a single category.

options.text: A fingerprint plus a face scan
options.rationale: Both are things you are: one category.

questions.explanation: MFA requires two or more different factor categories: something you know, have, or are. Two passwords, a password plus a security question, or two biometrics all stay within one category.
questions.discriminator_tested: MFA needs different factor categories.

questions.stem: A bank's administrators receive their one-time sign-in codes by SMS. Which change BEST strengthens this second factor?

options.text: A time-based code from an authenticator app or token
options.rationale: Correct: generated on the device, so it can't be intercepted in transit or redirected.

options.text: Longer SMS codes that expire sooner
options.rationale: Slightly better, but SMS can still be intercepted or redirected.

options.text: A voice call that reads out the code
options.rationale: Voice codes can be redirected just like SMS.

options.text: A second password entered after the first
options.rationale: Two passwords isn't MFA at all.

questions.explanation: MFA methods include email, SMS, voice calls, and time-based hardware or software tokens. Time-based tokens are generally stronger; SMS, voice, and email codes can be intercepted or redirected, for example by SIM swapping.
questions.discriminator_tested: Time-based tokens are stronger than SMS, voice, or email codes.

questions.stem: User jtan is logged in to a router but can't enter configuration mode. The AAA server's log is below. Which AAA function stopped the command?
questions.exhibit:
10:14:02  user=jtan  cmd="show running-config"   author=PASS
10:14:20  user=jtan  cmd="configure terminal"     author=FAIL
10:14:20  user=jtan  session still active

options.text: Authorization
options.rationale: Correct: the per-command check decided what jtan may do.

options.text: Authentication
options.rationale: jtan's login already succeeded.

options.text: Accounting
options.rationale: Accounting records commands; it doesn't block them.

options.text: Identification
options.rationale: The user was already identified as jtan.

questions.explanation: Authorization determines what an authenticated user may access or do, and it happens after authentication. jtan's login succeeded; the per-command check denied configuration mode.
questions.discriminator_tested: Authorization happens after authentication.

questions.stem: An HR-driven system creates accounts when people are hired, changes their access when they transfer, and disables everything when they leave, across 40 applications. What BEST describes this program?

options.text: Identity and access management over the account lifecycle
options.rationale: Correct: managing identities and access from joiner to leaver.

options.text: Centralized AAA through a RADIUS server
options.rationale: One mechanism IAM might use, not the program itself.

options.text: Role-based access control for each application
options.rationale: Roles may be part of it, but the lifecycle program is broader.

options.text: Accounting of what users did in each application
options.rationale: Accounting records activity; it doesn't create or remove access.

questions.explanation: Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the processes and tools that manage identities and their access across their lifecycle. It is the umbrella program; AAA is one mechanism inside it.
questions.discriminator_tested: IAM is the umbrella program; AAA is one mechanism inside it.

questions.stem: A help-desk technician needs to reset users' passwords. Which access BEST follows least privilege?

options.text: A delegated role scoped to that one task
options.rationale: Correct: exactly the access the job needs.

options.text: Account operator rights over the whole directory
options.rationale: Would work, but grants far more than password resets.

options.text: Domain admin rights with full activity logging
options.rationale: Logging records misuse but doesn't limit the access.

options.text: The admin's shared password for emergencies
options.rationale: Shared admin credentials violate least privilege and accountability.

questions.explanation: Least privilege grants only the access needed to do the job. It limits the damage from mistakes, malware, and insiders; logging records misuse but doesn't limit it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Grant only the access needed to do the job.

questions.stem: A hospital system manages access as shown below. User amorales moves from a nursing position to a physician position. What is the BEST change?
questions.exhibit:
Role Nurse      -> read: patient-chart   write: vitals
Role Physician  -> read: patient-chart   write: orders, prescriptions
User amorales   -> roles: Nurse
User bpatel     -> roles: Physician, Nurse

options.text: Assign amorales the Physician role
options.rationale: Correct: access follows the role.

options.text: Grant amorales write access to orders directly
options.rationale: Would work, but bypasses the role model and drifts out of sync.

options.text: Edit the Nurse role to include prescriptions
options.rationale: That changes access for every nurse.

options.text: Create a second account for amorales as a physician
options.rationale: Duplicate accounts weaken accountability.

questions.explanation: In RBAC, permissions attach to roles and users get access through their role, not through per-individual assignment. Changing jobs means changing roles; editing a role changes everyone who holds it.
questions.discriminator_tested: RBAC is role-based, not per-individual.

questions.stem: After an outage, the team needs to know which administrator changed a router's routing table, and when. Which AAA function provides this?

options.text: Accounting
options.rationale: Correct: the record of who did what and when.

options.text: Authorization
options.rationale: Authorization decided whether the change was allowed; it doesn't record it.

options.text: Authentication
options.rationale: Authentication proved who logged in, not what they changed.

options.text: Identification
options.rationale: Identification is the claim of identity at login.

questions.explanation: Accounting records who did what and when (logins, commands, session data). It is the after-the-fact audit trail that enables traceability.
questions.discriminator_tested: Accounting is the after-the-fact audit trail.

questions.stem: A company needs open-standard, centralized authentication for 2,000 users on 802.1X Wi-Fi and its VPN. Which AAA protocol BEST fits?

options.text: RADIUS
options.rationale: Correct: the open standard for network access.

options.text: TACACS+
options.rationale: Cisco-originated and typical for device administration, not user network access.

options.text: Kerberos
options.rationale: A ticket system for domain logins, not 802.1X Wi-Fi authentication.

options.text: Local accounts on each AP
options.rationale: Not centralized; doesn't scale to 2,000 users.

questions.explanation: RADIUS provides centralized AAA over UDP 1812 (authentication) and 1813 (accounting). It is an open standard that combines authentication and authorization, typical for network access: 802.1X, Wi-Fi, and VPN.
questions.discriminator_tested: RADIUS: open standard, typical for network access.

questions.stem: A capture shows two AAA sessions, summarized below. The security team prefers the protocol in session B for administering switches. What BEST explains why?
questions.exhibit:
Session A:  UDP 1812  Access-Request  User-Name=jtan  User-Password=<hidden>
            NAS-IP-Address=10.1.1.2  (other attributes readable)
Session B:  TCP 49    TACACS+ packet   body=<encrypted>

options.text: It encrypts the whole payload and splits the three As
options.rationale: Correct: full encryption and separate authorization allow per-command control.

options.text: It runs over TCP, so delivery is reliable
options.rationale: True, but reliability isn't the security reason.

options.text: It encrypts just the password, like RADIUS
options.rationale: That describes session A; session B hides the whole body.

options.text: It is an open standard used for Wi-Fi access
options.rationale: That describes RADIUS.

questions.explanation: TACACS+ is Cisco-originated AAA over TCP 49 that encrypts the entire payload and separates authentication, authorization, and accounting, allowing per-command control, so it is typical for device administration. RADIUS encrypts only the password.
questions.discriminator_tested: TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload and separates the three As.

questions.stem: A router is configured as shown below. The TACACS+ server is reachable but rejects an admin's password. What BEST describes what happens?
questions.exhibit:
aaa new-model
tacacs server TAC1
 address ipv4 10.1.9.20
 key 7 0822455D0A16
aaa authentication login VTY-LOGIN group tacacs+ local
!
line vty 0 4
 login authentication VTY-LOGIN

options.text: Login fails; local is used when the server is down
options.rationale: Correct: a rejection ends the list; fallback is for an unreachable server.

options.text: The admin's login attempt is denied
options.rationale: True, but it misses why the local accounts aren't tried.

options.text: The router retries with the local accounts
options.rationale: A rejection isn't an error, so the next method isn't tried.

options.text: The router prompts for the enable password instead
options.rationale: Enable isn't in this method list.

questions.explanation: Configuring iAAA means enabling AAA, defining the server, building method lists, and applying them to lines. Method-list order matters: fallback to local happens when the server is unreachable (an error), not when it rejects the credentials.
questions.discriminator_tested: Fallback to local happens when the server is unreachable, not when it rejects.

questions.stem: A laptop joins an 802.1X Wi-Fi network that uses RADIUS. Which sequence of messages is correct?

options.text: User to AP, AP to RADIUS, RADIUS reply to AP
options.rationale: Correct: the AP is the RADIUS client.

options.text: User to RADIUS, RADIUS to AP, AP reply to user
options.rationale: The laptop doesn't talk to RADIUS directly.

options.text: AP to RADIUS, RADIUS to user, user reply to AP
options.rationale: RADIUS replies to the AP, not the user.

options.text: User to RADIUS, RADIUS reply to user, then AP
options.rationale: The user's device isn't a RADIUS client.

questions.explanation: In the RADIUS login process, the user's credentials go to the access device, which sends an Access-Request to the RADIUS server and acts on the Access-Accept, Access-Reject, or Access-Challenge. The access device (switch or AP) is the RADIUS client, not the user's endpoint.
questions.discriminator_tested: The access device is the RADIUS client.

questions.stem: Which password approach BEST resists guessing?

options.text: A random 20-character passphrase of words
options.rationale: Correct: length multiplies the search space.

options.text: A 10-character password mixing four character types
options.rationale: Complexity helps, but length adds more strength.

options.text: An 8-character password changed monthly
options.rationale: Frequent changes don't make a short password hard to guess.

options.text: A dictionary word with a number and symbol added
options.rationale: Predictable substitutions are in every cracking list.

questions.explanation: Longer passwords with mixed character types resist guessing, and length adds more strength than complexity alone: each extra character multiplies the search space, while predictable substitutions add little.
questions.discriminator_tested: Length adds more strength than complexity alone.

questions.stem: An attacker deliberately enters wrong passwords against each executive's account. With a lockout policy of five attempts, what is the MOST likely effect?

options.text: The executives are locked out, denying them service
options.rationale: Correct: the lockout itself becomes the attack.

options.text: The attacker's guessing is stopped after five tries
options.rationale: True, but the attacker wasn't trying to guess.

options.text: The attacker learns the executives' passwords
options.rationale: Wrong guesses reveal nothing.

options.text: The lockout policy is disabled automatically
options.rationale: Policies don't switch themselves off.

questions.explanation: Password lockout locks an account after a set number of failed attempts. It counters online brute force but can itself be abused to lock out legitimate users.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lockout counters brute force but can be abused to lock out users.

questions.stem: A user's PC on port Gi1/0/9 gets no network access. The switch shows the status below. What BEST explains it?
questions.exhibit:
Interface:   Gi1/0/9
Status:      Unauthorized
Allowed:     EAPOL only
Last event:  EAP timeout (no supplicant response)

options.text: The port passes only EAPOL until the PC authenticates
options.rationale: Correct: the PC never answered, so the port stays blocked.

options.text: The port is blocking the PC's traffic
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

options.text: The switch port is administratively shut down
options.rationale: A shut port wouldn't show EAPOL activity.

options.text: The PC was given a 169.254 address by the switch
options.rationale: Switches don't assign APIPA addresses.

questions.explanation: 802.1X is port-based access control: a port passes only authentication traffic (EAPOL) until the device authenticates. Here the PC never answered, so the port stays unauthorized.
questions.discriminator_tested: The port stays blocked until authentication succeeds.

questions.stem: In an 802.1X deployment, which component decides whether the user is allowed on, and which enforces that decision at the port?

options.text: The RADIUS server decides; the switch enforces
options.rationale: Correct: authentication server decides, authenticator enforces.

options.text: The switch decides; the RADIUS server enforces
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: The supplicant decides; the switch enforces
options.rationale: The supplicant is the client asking for access.

options.text: The switch decides and enforces; RADIUS logs
options.rationale: The decision comes from the authentication server.

questions.explanation: 802.1X components are the supplicant (client), the authenticator (switch or WAP), and the authentication server (RADIUS). The authenticator enforces; the server decides.
questions.discriminator_tested: The authenticator enforces; the server decides.

questions.stem: Which order BEST describes the NAC process for a device joining the network?

options.text: Connect, identify and assess, apply policy access
options.rationale: Correct: policy can only act on what was learned.

options.text: Connect, apply policy access, identify and assess
options.rationale: Access is set before anything is known about the device.

options.text: Identify and assess, connect, apply policy access
options.rationale: The device must connect before it can be assessed.

options.text: Apply policy access, connect, identify and assess
options.rationale: Policy can't apply to a device that hasn't connected.

questions.explanation: In the NAC process, a device connects, is identified and assessed, and then policy sets its access level: full, restricted, quarantine, or deny. The outcome need not be all-or-nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAC outcome is policy-driven and need not be all-or-nothing.

questions.stem: A NAC system shows the result below for a device that can't run an 802.1X client. Which NAC function produced it?
questions.exhibit:
MAC 00:1b:a9:3e:7c:11     OUI: Brother Industries
DHCP option 55: 1,3,6,15,44,47     hostname: BRN001BA93E7C11
Open ports: 515, 631, 9100
Result: Printer (confidence 92%)  -> policy: PRINTERS VLAN

options.text: Profiling
options.rationale: Correct: it worked out what the device is from observed attributes.

options.text: Posture assessment
options.rationale: Posture checks health such as patches and antivirus, not device type.

options.text: 802.1X authentication
options.rationale: The device can't run a supplicant.

options.text: Guest isolation
options.rationale: Isolation is a placement decision, not identification.

questions.explanation: Profiling identifies what a device is (its type or class) from observed attributes such as MAC vendor, DHCP options, and open ports. It suits devices that can't run a supplicant, such as printers and IoT devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: Profiling identifies device type; suits devices without a supplicant.

questions.stem: Profiling, posture assessment, and 802.1X authentication each answer a different question about a device. Which question does posture assessment answer?

options.text: Is the device healthy and compliant?
options.rationale: Correct: patches, antivirus, configuration.

options.text: What kind of device is it?
options.rationale: That is profiling.

options.text: Who is the user or device?
options.rationale: That is authentication.

options.text: Which VLAN did DHCP assign it?
options.rationale: DHCP doesn't assign VLANs.

questions.explanation: Posture assessment checks a device's health and compliance (patches, antivirus, configuration). It answers health, while authentication answers identity and profiling answers type.
questions.discriminator_tested: Health vs identity vs type.

questions.stem: A hospital will let staff use personal phones for email and the scheduling app. Which two controls BEST address the risk? (Choose two.)

options.text: Posture checks before granting access
options.rationale: Correct: unmanaged devices must meet a health baseline.

options.text: A segment that limits personal devices to approved apps
options.rationale: Correct: segmentation keeps them away from clinical systems.

options.text: A captive portal that encrypts their Wi-Fi traffic
options.rationale: A portal is a gate, not encryption.

options.text: Allowing personal devices on the clinical VLAN
options.rationale: The opposite of segmentation.

options.text: Training staff on phishing
options.rationale: Useful, but it doesn't address unmanaged devices on the network.

questions.explanation: BYOD means personally owned devices accessing organizational resources. Because they are unmanaged and varied, BYOD needs NAC, posture checks, and segmentation.
questions.discriminator_tested: BYOD is unmanaged and varied: needs NAC, posture, segmentation.

questions.stem: A hotel offers Wi-Fi to conference attendees. Which design BEST meets the goal of guest network isolation?

options.text: A separate segment with internet-only access
options.rationale: Correct: guests can't reach internal resources.

options.text: The staff network with a separate password
options.rationale: A different password still puts guests on the staff network.

options.text: A captive portal on the staff network
options.rationale: A portal gates entry but doesn't isolate guests.

options.text: WPA3 on the staff network to stop snooping
options.rationale: Encryption doesn't separate guests from internal systems.

questions.explanation: Guest network isolation places guests on a separate segment with internet-only access, isolated from internal resources.
questions.discriminator_tested: Guest isolation = separate segment, internet-only.

questions.stem: A cafe's Wi-Fi shows a terms page before allowing internet access. A customer assumes the page means their traffic is now encrypted. What BEST describes the page?

options.text: A gate for access, not encryption of traffic
options.rationale: Correct: it controls entry; the network may still be open.

options.text: A login page that records who accepted the terms
options.rationale: Often true, but it doesn't address the encryption assumption.

options.text: A WPA3 handshake shown as a web page
options.rationale: Wi-Fi encryption happens before any web page.

options.text: A VPN that starts when terms are accepted
options.rationale: Accepting terms doesn't start a VPN.

questions.explanation: A captive portal intercepts a new user's first request and requires login or acceptance before granting access. It is a gate for guest and BYOD onboarding, not encryption of wireless traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: Captive portal is a gate, not encryption.
